transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hi everyone thanks for joining, we'll get started in a minute.
[00:12] Emily (Zephyr - ML Lead): Yep thanks, excited to dig in, we want the 6B model to run in-prod with 95th p99 latency under 300ms for single turn, and cost targets that keep inference under our current budget.
[00:35] Samir (Redwood SE): Cool, quick agenda: quantization options — INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ — then we'll map those to latency/throughput and accuracy; also batching/KV cache impacts and VPC/on-prem notes.
[01:05] Raj (Zephyr - Infra): For our infra, we have on-prem A100s and a VPC in GCP with T4s for dev. We care about kernel compatibility and whether Redwood's runtime will pick the right kernels automatically.
[01:28] Samir: Right, so starting with INT8. INT8 (symmetric/affine calibration) gives big perf wins on tensor cores but needs careful calibration; on-house quantizers historically see 2-4% LM loss on downstream QA tasks — sometimes more depending on layerwise distribution. GPTQ & AWQ are post-training quantizers designed to reduce that error; GPTQ minimizes MSE per-block but can still produce outliers on attention projections.
[02:10] Emily: We're especially worried about accuracy regressions on our summarization prompts — users notice hallucinations easily.
[02:22] Samir: For summarization, we usually recommend GPTQ with per-channel second-order corrections, or AWQ which trades a bit more compute during quantize time but tends to keep logits closer. In our internal benchmarks on a 6B LLaMA-style model, GPTQ had a 1.8% drop on ROUGE-L vs FP16; AWQ was 1.1% but required a slightly larger dequant correction table.
[03:05] Alex: And on the runtime side — AWQ tends to map well to INT8 kernels with small additional overhead for dequant ops; FP8 offers a middle ground where compute benefits are there but ecosystem/kernel support varies (NVIDIA's newer runtimes, Ampere/Hopper have FP8 HW accel but it's less common in open kernels).
[03:44] Raj: So for our on-prem A100 fleet, we should get good INT8 throughput — what about KV cache? Does INT8 affect KV cache memory footprint or hit behavior?
[04:00] Samir: Good question. Quantizing the KV cache reduces memory per entry (e.g., FP16->INT8 halves or better). But you must be careful: quantization noise can lead to degraded attention scores, especially for long contexts, so we sometimes preserve KV in FP16 for the first N layers and quantize later layers — hybrid approach.
[04:38] Emily: What's the tradeoff to keep first N layers as FP16? Memory cost?
[04:45] Samir: Yes memory + bandwidth; hybrid reduces memory savings but preserves important attention fidelity. In our tests keeping first 4 layers FP16 and rest INT8 kept ROUGE within 0.7% of FP16, while reducing KV memory by ~60%.
[05:12] Alex: Batching strategy: small batch sizes (1-4) with micro-batching and dynamic batching window gives best p99 latency; for throughput, larger batch sizes with async KV cache help. Redwood runtime supports continuous batching with latency SLOs — you can set per-route SLOs and it will limit batch waiting time.
[05:48] Raj: On the VPC side, if we run in our GCP VPC with Redwood Private, what are kernel dependencies? Will we need to install special drivers or container images?
[05:58] Samir: We provide hardened images for on-prem and VPC deploys; for on-prem you need CUDA 11.8+ and specific cuBLAS/cuDNN versions; for FP8 you'd need newer libcudnn that exposes FP8 kernels. We also recommend pinned NCCL versions. We'll share a runbook.
[06:28] Marta (Zephyr - Security): For security, we need to see KMS integrations and attestations; also SOC2 reports.
[06:36] Alex: We'll attach SOC2 + KMS integration docs; Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs, and we can enable strict RBAC.
[06:50] Emily: Back to accuracy — what's your suggested regression threshold for us? We measure ROUGE and task-specific exact match.
[06:59] Samir: For customer-facing summarization, customers typically accept up to 1% absolute drop in ROUGE-L; above that we recommend AWQ or mixed precision + fine-tune or quantization-aware calibration.
[07:20] Emily: If AWQ only gives 1.1% drop, that's probably okay. But can we run A/B tests to be safe?
[07:28] Alex: Yes, we can do canary rollout with Redwood's rollout policy — route 10% traffic to quantized model and monitor quality metrics.
[07:40] Raj: For benchmarking, can you run tests that include our VPC latencies and on-prem raw throughput numbers, and also simulate our real prompt distribution?
[07:51] Samir: Yes we'll run end-to-end benchmarks including network egress latencies for VPC and raw p50/p95/p99 for on-prem. Need your prompt samples and a few representative model inputs.
[08:08] Emily: We'll share a 1k prompt set; and we'd like to include some long-context tests — up to 8k tokens.
[08:16] Samir: Note that long-context + quantization increases risk; KV quantization errors accumulate. We'll include hybrid KV approaches and a config that keeps key/values in FP16 for longer contexts.
[08:36] Alex: Anything else on model artifacts? Access patterns?  
[08:42] Emily: We'll provide s3 access and temporary credentials. Security will vet those.
[08:48] Marta: Also need a data processing agreement for model weights sharing — legal will handle.
[08:54] Alex: Understood.
[09:00] Samir: Quick note on kernels: for A100 we recommend patched cutlass kernels for INT8 GEMMs; on Hopper there's native FP8 in cuBLAS for certain data types. The runtime auto-selects kernels but we can force flags if you have strict driver constraints.
[09:28] Raj: Good — we'll collect driver versions.  
[09:35] Emily: Timeline — if we provide prompts and access by Friday, can you have a baseline by next Wednesday?
[09:45] Alex: Yes, we'll aim for GPTQ baseline + initial AWQ runs by next Wednesday.
[09:52] Samir: We'll include per-prompt accuracy deltas, batch configs, KV hybrid settings, and kernel flags in the spreadsheet.
[10:02] Alex: Ok quick recap of next steps and owners...
[10:10] Emily: Great thanks everyone.
[10:15] Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and docs.
